secondaryCondition: Lumbosacral radiculopathy (nerve-root compression and irritation from a herniated/degenerated disc)
secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.124a, DC 8520 (sciatic nerve) with DC 8620 (neuritis) or DC 8720 (neuralgia); DC 8526 for a femoral/L4 distribution; wholly sensory involvement is capped at the mild, or at most the moderate, degree under the § 4.124a peripheral-nerve preface; evaluate any superimposed joint limitation of motion under the appropriate § 4.71a joint code with § 4.59
primaryCondition: Degenerative disc disease of the lumbar spine (intervertebral disc syndrome)
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.71a, DC 5243 (intervertebral disc syndrome — assign only where there is disc herniation with compression and/or irritation of the adjacent nerve root) or DC 5242 (degenerative arthritis, degenerative disc disease other than intervertebral disc syndrome); rate under the General Rating Formula for Diseases and Injuries of the Spine or the Formula for Rating Intervertebral Disc Syndrome Based on Incapacitating Episodes, whichever yields the higher evaluation
etiologicalMechanism: ANATOMY AND THE MECHANICAL ARM. The intervertebral disc is a hydraulic structure in which the annulus fibrosus confines a proteoglycan-rich nucleus pulposus. Degenerative disc disease is defined by loss of proteoglycan and water content, annular tears and radial fissuring, loss of disc height, and adaptive change in the endplates and facet joints. Once annular competence is lost, nuclear material migrates posterolaterally into the lateral recess or the intervertebral foramen, the two locations where the traversing or exiting nerve root has the least reserve of space. Radiculopathy is not simple mechanical crushing. Compression of the dorsal root ganglion renders it mechanosensitive and causes ectopic, high-frequency discharges from an already sensitised membrane, which is why radicular pain is lancinating, dermatomal and reproducible with specific postures and manoeuvres rather than the dull, axial, load-dependent pain of a discogenic back. THE BIOCHEMICAL ARM. The exposed nerve root is simultaneously bathed in nucleus pulposus-derived inflammatory mediators. Olmarker and Larsson demonstrated experimentally that application of autologous nucleus pulposus to a spinal nerve root produces structural nerve-root injury and intraneural oedema, and that tumour necrosis factor-alpha is a necessary mediator of that injury because selective TNF-alpha inhibition substantially reduces it. This is the biochemical half of the nexus: it explains why radicular pain can be severe out of proportion to the size of the compression on imaging, why a herniation can produce symptoms before it becomes a large compressive mass, and why inflammation — not only displacement — predicts the radicular syndrome. THE REGULATORY BRIDGE. The rating schedule itself conditions the primary evaluation on the causal fact. Section 4.71a, DC 5243, may be assigned only where there is disc herniation with compression and/or irritation of the adjacent nerve root; DC 5242 is reserved for all other disc diagnoses. A veteran whose service-connected disc disease is rated under DC 5243 therefore already has an adjudicative finding that the disc is compressing or irritating an adjacent nerve root, which is the same finding that establishes the nexus to the radicular syndrome. Section 4.71a, General Rating Formula for Diseases and Injuries of the Spine, Note (1), then directs that associated objective neurologic abnormalities be evaluated separately under an appropriate diagnostic code. That Note, read with § 4.14, means the radiculopathy may be rated separately under § 4.124a provided the identical signs and symptoms are not used to support both evaluations: sensory loss and reflex change supporting the nerve rating must not simultaneously be the manifestations relied upon for the 20/10 percent spine step. SECTION 3.310(a) ANALYSIS. This is a straight proximate-cause question under § 3.310(a), not aggravation under § 3.310(b) and not a treatment side effect. The causal chain is a single unbroken physiological sequence — service-connected disc degeneration, then annular failure and nuclear migration, then nerve-root compression and TNF-alpha-mediated root inflammation, then dermatomal pain, sensory loss, reflex attenuation and, in more advanced cases, weakness and atrophy. The secondary condition is considered part of the original condition once service connection is granted. MEETING THE AT LEAST AS LIKELY AS NOT STANDARD. The opinion should be able to state, and should be required to demonstrate, four independent supports: (1) a service-connected lumbar disc disorder rated under DC 5242/5243 with the relevant level identified; (2) cross-sectional imaging showing disc material contacting or displacing the nerve root at a level that anatomically corresponds; (3) a clinical pattern concordant with that same level — dermatomal pain or sensory loss, a matching myotomal strength deficit, and a matching reflex change (L4 to the patellar reflex and tibialis anterior, L5 to extensor hallucis longus and dorsiflexion, S1 to the Achilles reflex and plantar flexion) — and, where available, corroborative electrodiagnostic evidence; and (4) a reasoned exclusion of competing causes, specifically diabetic or other metabolic polyneuropathy, spinal stenosis at a different level, vascular claudication, piriformis entrapment, malignancy, and unrelated peripheral nerve entrapment. Where the level shown on imaging does not match the distribution of symptoms, or where a competing polyneuropathy is present, the nexus statement should not be given in a simple causation form. LIMITATIONS DISCLOSED ON THE FACE OF THE OPINION. First, the Olmarker and Larsson study is an experimental animal model; it establishes a mechanism and a mediator, not individual human causation, and it should be described that way. Second, the SPORT observational cohort is non-randomised, its treatment assignment was by patient choice, and its outcomes were self-reported, so it is subject to confounding; its own abstract notes that the companion randomised trial found intent-to-treat differences in favour of discectomy that were not statistically significant because more than half of the participants crossed over between arms. The scientific inference from that cohort is therefore limited to the proposition that surgical removal of the compressing disc is followed by greater improvement in sciatica and function than continued non-operative care in patients who elect surgery, and it must be presented with that limitation attached. Third, this mapping is a knowledge-base hypothesis; it does not adjudicate any individual claim, and the diagnostic codes cited must be confirmed by a qualified rating specialist against the current schedule before they are relied upon.

medicalEvidence.title: CLINICAL PRACTICE. Herniated Lumbar Intervertebral Disk.
medicalEvidence.summary: Authoritative New England Journal of Medicine clinical review of the herniated lumbar disc, covering the anatomy and pathophysiology of annular failure, the mechanism by which nuclear material compresses and chemically irritates the nerve root, the resulting radicular syndrome, the natural history (including the high rate of spontaneous improvement), and the indications for discectomy. Used here as the doctrinal clinical statement of the disc-to-nerve-root causal sequence and of the natural-history baseline against which any claimed progression must be measured. Note that this is a narrative clinical review and carries no abstract and no original data.

medicalEvidence.title: Tumor necrosis factor alpha and nucleus-pulposus-induced nerve root injury.
medicalEvidence.summary: Experimental demonstration that autologous nucleus pulposus applied to a spinal nerve root causes structural nerve-root injury and intraneural oedema, and that tumour necrosis factor-alpha is a mediator of that injury: selective TNF-alpha inhibition substantially reduced the injury. This is the biochemical arm of the nexus and shows that radicular injury is inflammatory and not only compressive. LIMITATION, disclosed: the study is an animal model; it establishes mechanism and mediator, not individual human causation.

medicalEvidence.title: Surgical vs nonoperative treatment for lumbar disk herniation: the Spine Patient Outcomes Research Trial (SPORT) observational cohort.
medicalEvidence.authors: Weinstein JN, Lurie JD, Tosteson TD, Skinner JS, Hanscom B, Tosteson AN, Herkowitz H, Fischgrund J, Cammisa FP, Albert T, Deyo RA
medicalEvidence.summary: Prospective cohort of 743 surgical candidates with imaging-confirmed lumbar disc herniation and persistent sciatica; 528 chose discectomy and 191 chose usual non-operative care. Patients who underwent removal of the compressing disc reported substantially greater improvement in bodily pain (treatment effect 14.8, 95% CI 10.8-18.9 at 3 months; 10.2, 95% CI 5.9-14.5 at 2 years), physical function (15.4, 95% CI 11.6-19.2) and Oswestry Disability Index -15.2 (95% CI -18.5 to -11.8), narrowing but persisting at 2 years. Cited as intervention-response evidence that relieving the disc-nerve-root interface relieves the radicular syndrome. LIMITATIONS, disclosed: the cohort is non-randomised with treatment self-selected and outcomes self-reported, and the paper states that the companion randomised trial's intent-to-treat difference was not statistically significant because of extensive crossover; inference must be limited accordingly.

secondaryCondition: Carpal tunnel syndrome (median nerve compression neuropathy)
secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.124a, DC 8515 (median nerve, incomplete paralysis) with DC 8615 (neuritis) or DC 8715 (neuralgia); wholly sensory involvement should be rated at the mild, or at most the moderate, degree under the § 4.124a peripheral-nerve preface; no separate 38 CFR Part 4 code exists for entrapment neuropathy as such
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.119, DC 7903 (hypothyroidism) — 100 percent where manifesting as myxedema, otherwise 30 percent, with residual effects thereafter rated under the appropriate codes of the affected body system per Notes (1) and (2) to DC 7903
etiologicalMechanism: THE MECHANISM THAT COULD ESTABLISH THE NEXUS. The carpal tunnel is a rigid osteofibrous compartment bounded dorsally by the carpal bones and volarly by the transverse carpal ligament, and it has essentially no capacity to expand. In severe or inadequately treated hypothyroidism, thyroid hormone deficiency produces diffuse extracellular accumulation of glycosaminoglycans and mucopolysaccharide-rich ground substance — the histological basis of myxedema — within the flexor retinaculum, the flexor tendon sheaths and the subsynovial connective tissue of the canal. The result is thickening of the retinaculum and enlargement of the canal contents within a fixed cross-sectional area, which raises carpal canal pressure. Sustained elevation of canal pressure above the capillary perfusion threshold of the median nerve produces intraneural ischaemia, impaired axonal transport, and eventually focal demyelination, manifested as nocturnal burning and paraesthesias in the median distribution, then thenar weakness and abductor pollicis brevis atrophy. The mechanism is biologically coherent, parallels the well-established association of carpal tunnel syndrome with other states of connective-tissue infiltration and fluid retention (pregnancy, obesity, diabetes mellitus, acromegaly, amyloidosis), and is the mechanism on which a hypothyroid causation opinion would have to rest. It is also a mechanism that predicts the correct chronology: symptoms should arise during a period of active or untreated thyroid deficiency, and should improve with adequate replacement therapy, because the glycosaminoglycan deposition is to a substantial degree reversible. THE EVIDENCE, STATED HONESTLY. The population-level evidence does not support a general statement that hypothyroidism causes carpal tunnel syndrome. The meta-analysis of 18 studies found an unadjusted association for thyroid disease (effect size 1.32, 95% CI 1.04-1.68) and for hypothyroidism (2.15, 95% CI 1.64-2.83), but after adjustment for confounders the association for thyroid disease disappeared (1.17, 95% CI 0.71-1.92) and the hypothyroidism estimate attenuated to a modest residual 1.44 (95% CI 1.27-1.63); the author identified publication bias and concluded that confounding and publication bias may account for part of the remaining excess. A Mendelian randomisation study reported statistically significant causal estimates, but the effect sizes were very small (hypothyroidism OR 1.04, 95% CI 1.01-1.08; hyperthyroidism OR 1.08, 95% CI 1.05-1.12) and such estimates reflect lifelong genetically instrumented liability, not an individual veteran's clinical thyroid disease. A single-centre cross-sectional study of 422 carpal tunnel release patients found hypothyroidism in 13.8 percent, but more than two thirds of those patients were asymptomatic from a thyroid standpoint and the presence of thyroid abnormality did not affect the duration of carpal tunnel symptoms — findings that cut against, not for, the nexus in the individual case. SECTION 3.310(a) ANALYSIS AND THE AT LEAST AS LIKELY AS NOT STANDARD. Because the population data are modest and confound-sensitive, this mapping should not be advanced as generic causation. To reach the at least as likely as not threshold an opinion must supply individual proof of the specific mechanism: (1) a service-connected hypothyroid state documented as active or inadequately treated at or immediately before the onset of the median nerve symptoms, with supporting laboratory values (elevated thyroid-stimulating hormone with low free thyroxine); (2) clinical or documented evidence of the myxedematous state itself — periorbital or pretibial non-pitting oedema, macroglossia, hoarseness, dry skin, slow-relaxing reflexes, or diffuse soft-tissue thickening — because it is the infiltrative state, not the laboratory diagnosis alone, that occludes the canal; (3) improvement or resolution of the median nerve symptoms after adequate thyroid hormone replacement, which is the single most probative piece of individual evidence available in this route; (4) exclusion of the competing causes that carry far larger attributable weight in the general population — diabetes mellitus, obesity and increased body mass index, pregnancy, rheumatoid arthritis and other inflammatory arthropathies, acromegaly, amyloidosis, prior wrist fracture or dislocation, vibratory tool exposure and repetitive forceful wrist use; and (5) a coherent latency, that is, an interval consistent with gradual canal volume change rather than symptoms that began years before any thyroid abnormality or long after it was corrected. PYRIMIDING AND OVERLAP. Section 4.14 must be considered in both directions here. If the myxedematous soft-tissue proliferation is already being used to support a rating under DC 7903 or another code, or if a neuropathy is already rated as a residual of the endocrine disease, the same manifestations may not be rated again as carpal tunnel syndrome; conversely, if the median nerve findings are clearly separable from the thyroid residuals they may be rated separately under § 4.124a. LIMITATIONS DISCLOSED ON THE FACE OF THE OPINION. First, no located study demonstrates that thyroid status, rather than shared metabolic risk factors, accounts for the association; the adjusted meta-analytic estimate is weak and the Mendelian randomisation estimates are clinically trivial in magnitude. Second, one included series found thyroid abnormality did not alter symptom duration, so duration should not be offered as corroboration. Third, the glycosaminoglycan-deposition mechanism is textbook explanatory pathophysiology rather than a finding measured in a hypothyroid carpal tunnel cohort, and it must be presented as mechanism rather than as direct experimental demonstration. Fourth, this mapping is a knowledge-base hypothesis only; it does not adjudicate an individual claim and the diagnostic codes must be confirmed by a qualified rating specialist against the current schedule before reliance.

medicalEvidence.title: Hypothyroidism and carpal tunnel syndrome: a meta-analysis.
medicalEvidence.summary: Meta-analysis of 18 studies. Unadjusted estimates showed an association of thyroid disease with carpal tunnel syndrome (effect size 1.32, 95% CI 1.04-1.68) and a stronger one for hypothyroidism (2.15, 95% CI 1.64-2.83). After adjustment for confounders the thyroid disease association disappeared (1.17, 95% CI 0.71-1.92) and the hypothyroidism estimate attenuated to a modest residual (1.44, 95% CI 1.27-1.63); the author found evidence of publication bias and concluded that confounding and publication bias may account for part of the remaining excess. Cited precisely because it is the strongest available synthesis and it does not support generic causation.

medicalEvidence.title: The causal relationship between thyroid dysfunction and carpal tunnel syndrome: A Mendelian randomization study.
medicalEvidence.authors: Zhang F, Cui R, Yin L, Bi R, Xu H, Wang S
medicalEvidence.summary: Two-sample Mendelian randomisation analysis reporting statistically significant causal estimates for hypothyroidism (inverse-variance weighted odds ratio 1.04, 95% CI 1.01-1.08) and hyperthyroidism (odds ratio 1.08, 95% CI 1.05-1.12) with no detected pleiotropy. Supports a genuine directional effect but with clinically trivial effect sizes; the estimates also reflect lifelong genetically instrumented liability rather than an individual veteran's treated or untreated clinical thyroid disease. Disclosed accordingly.

medicalEvidence.title: Prevalence of Hypothyroidism Among Carpal Tunnel Syndrome Patients at a Hospital in Saudi Arabia.
medicalEvidence.authors: Aldaghri F, Algahtani MS, Almutairi TA, Albusair M, Bin Ghali K, Al Asim FS
medicalEvidence.summary: Cross-sectional study of 422 patients undergoing carpal tunnel release: 13.8 percent had hypothyroidism and 5 percent subclinical hypothyroidism, but more than two thirds of the hypothyroid patients were asymptomatic from a thyroid standpoint, the presence of a thyroid abnormality did not affect the duration of carpal tunnel symptoms, and body mass index was significantly associated with hypothyroidism (P = 0.001). Uses: establishes the co-prevalence and, more importantly, the confounding by body mass index; cited against the nexus as much as for it. LIMITATIONS, disclosed: single centre, retrospective and cross-sectional design with convenience sampling, no causal inference possible.

cfrCitations: 38 CFR § 4.119 (DC 7903 and its residual-rating Notes (1) and (2))

secondaryCondition: Peptic ulcer disease (gastric or duodenal ulcer, including NSAID-induced ulceration and bleeding)
secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.114, DC 7304 (peptic ulcer disease) — 100 percent post-operatively for perforation or hemorrhage for three months, thereafter 60/40/20/0 percent on residuals; NSAID-related mucosal disease without a frank ulcer is rated under DC 7307 (chronic gastritis), which expressly includes drug-induced gastritis and is rated as peptic ulcer disease
primaryCondition: Osteoarthritis of a major joint or joints on prescribed long-term non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug therapy
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.71a, DC 5003 (degenerative arthritis, other than post-traumatic) — rated on limitation of motion under the diagnostic code for the specific joint involved, with 10 or 20 percent for X-ray evidence of major joint involvement where limitation of motion is noncompensable
etiologicalMechanism: THE TWO ARMS OF NSAID GASTRODUODENAL INJURY. (1) Topical injury. Most non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are weak acids. In the acidic environment of the gastric lumen they remain un-ionised and lipid-soluble, diffuse freely across the mucous gel and the apical membrane of the surface epithelial cell, and then become trapped and ionised within the neutral intracellular compartment — the phenomenon of ion trapping. The result is intracellular acidification, mitochondrial injury with collapse of ATP production, loss of the cell's ability to maintain its bicarbonate-rich mucus barrier, and superficial epithelial necrosis. This arm acts within minutes of ingestion and is independent of prostaglandin synthesis. (2) Systemic injury. Once absorbed, NSAIDs inhibit cyclo-oxygenase-1 in the gastroduodenal mucosa, depleting prostaglandin E2 and prostacyclin. Because those prostaglandins tonically drive mucus and bicarbonate secretion and maintain mucosal blood flow through the submucosal plexus, their loss produces a mucosa that is simultaneously less protected and less able to repair. This is the arm responsible for the deeper lesions — true ulcers, and ulcers that bleed or perforate — and it can occur at any point on the dosing interval and even with a partially enteric-coated or rectally administered drug, because it is not a local contact effect. The two arms are additive, and a frank ulcer typically represents prostaglandin depletion superimposed on an epithelium already made vulnerable by topical injury. (3) Synergy with Helicobacter pylori. The meta-analytic evidence establishes that H. pylori infection and NSAID use are independent risk factors that act synergistically rather than as alternatives: in controlled studies, peptic ulcer disease was present in 138 of 385 NSAID takers (35.8 percent) against 23 of 276 controls (8.3 percent); the risk in H. pylori-infected NSAID takers relative to uninfected non-takers was 61.1 (95 percent CI 9.98-373); H. pylori infection multiplied the risk attributable to NSAID use by 3.53, and NSAID use multiplied the risk attributable to H. pylori infection by 3.55; and while H. pylori and NSAIDs increased the risk of ulcer bleeding by 1.79-fold and 4.85-fold respectively, the risk rose to 6.13-fold when both factors were present. (4) Dose, duration and co-factor multipliers. Strongly increased risk is concentrated in chronic use, in higher doses, in age over 60, in a prior ulcer history, in concomitant glucocorticoid, anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy, in smoking, and in serious systemic comorbidity. (5) Intervention-response corroboration. Because a proton pump inhibitor restores intragastric pH and therefore interrupts the topical ion-trapping arm as well as the acid-dependent component of ulcer propagation, the finding that prophylactic proton pump inhibition reduces incident NSAID-induced ulcers by roughly 71 percent (risk ratio 0.29, 95 percent CI 0.23-0.36, moderate-certainty evidence) is direct evidence that acid-dependent NSAID mucosal injury is a preventable causal process and not merely a coexisting finding. SECTION 3.310(a) ANALYSIS. This is a treatment side effect pleaded as proximate causation under § 3.310(a), not aggravation under § 3.310(b): service-connected osteoarthritis requires continuous prescription NSAID therapy, that therapy injures the gastroduodenal mucosa by the two mechanisms above, and the ulcer is the direct consequence. It is also the analytic posture that makes the claim susceptible to attack, because the statutory requirement is that the disability be the result of the service-connected disease or its treatment, and the treatment itself was prescribed. Section 3.310(a) does not distinguish between a disease and its required treatment: disability that is proximately due to or the result of a service-connected disability includes the foreseeable consequences of the treatment VA or a treating provider prescribes for it, and the medications taken for a service-connected arthritis are part of that disability's management. MEETING THE AT LEAST AS LIKELY AS NOT STANDARD. The opinion must establish: (1) a service-connected arthritic disability rated under DC 5003 with objective evidence of the joint involvement; (2) a documented prescription trail for a NSAID at therapeutic dose over a sustained period immediately preceding the ulcer, with the drug, dose and duration identified — a self-directed over-the-counter regimen is far weaker because it removes the treatment-of-the-service-connected-disability link; (3) endoscopic or imaging documentation of the ulcer or of ulcer-related bleeding as required by DC 7304's 0 percent floor (history of peptic ulcer disease documented by endoscopy or diagnostic imaging studies), because an uninvestigated dyspepsia syndrome will not support the rating even if the causal reasoning is sound; (4) temporally coherent onset and, ideally, improvement after the NSAID is withdrawn or after proton pump inhibitor prophylaxis is started; and (5) explicit handling of H. pylori, since the same meta-analysis attributes a larger share of population risk to H. pylori (48 percent) than to NSAIDs (24 percent) in attributable-risk modelling, with smoking contributing 23 percent. Where H. pylori infection has been documented and treated, the nexus opinion must explain why the NSAID exposure is still judged to have contributed — the synergism data support that conclusion — rather than ignoring the organism. Competing and contributing causes that must be addressed rather than omitted include H. pylori gastritis, alcohol use, smoking, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, stress-related mucosal disease in a critically ill patient, antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy, and systemic mastocytosis or other hypersecretory states. LIMITATIONS DISCLOSED ON THE FACE OF THE OPINION. First, attributable-risk modelling yields a population fraction, not an individual probability, and cannot by itself establish that a given veteran's ulcer was drug-induced; the individual proof must come from exposure chronology, endoscopy, response to withdrawal, and exclusion of competing causes. Second, the Cochrane review's certainty of evidence was downgraded: the dyspepsia symptom outcome was of very low certainty, the incident-ulcer outcome moderate, and the ulcer-complication outcome low (risk ratio 0.33, 95 percent CI 0.10-1.07, crossing unity), so the prophylaxis data support the causal process but do not quantify individual risk and should not be used to predict a specific veteran's course. Third, the review found that proton pump inhibitors may have little or no effect on dyspepsia as a dichotomous outcome, which means symptom relief is an unreliable surrogate and should not be offered as proof of causation. Fourth, this mapping is a knowledge-base hypothesis only; it does not adjudicate an individual claim, and the diagnostic codes must be confirmed by a qualified rating specialist against the current schedule before reliance.

medicalEvidence.title: Meta-analysis of risk factors for peptic ulcer. Nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs, Helicobacter pylori, and smoking.
medicalEvidence.summary: Attributable-risk meta-analysis of the three principal causes of peptic ulcer. Population attributable risk was estimated at 48 percent for Helicobacter pylori, 24 percent for non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and 23 percent for smoking, with 89 to 95 percent of ulcer-related serious upper gastrointestinal events attributable to those three factors. Used to establish that chronic NSAID exposure is an established independent cause of peptic ulcer disease, and simultaneously to frame the honest limitation that in population terms H. pylori carries the larger attributable share and must therefore be addressed rather than ignored in any individual nexus opinion. LIMITATION, disclosed: attributable-risk modelling yields a population fraction and cannot establish individual causation.

medicalEvidence.title: Role of Helicobacter pylori infection and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs in peptic-ulcer disease: a meta-analysis.
medicalEvidence.authors: Huang JQ, Sridhar S, Hunt RH
medicalEvidence.summary: Twenty-five observational studies. Uncomplicated peptic ulcer disease was more common in H. pylori-positive than H. pylori-negative NSAID takers (341 of 817, 41.7 percent, versus 209 of 808, 25.9 percent; odds ratio 2.12, 95 percent CI 1.68-2.67). In controlled studies ulcer disease was present in 138 of 385 NSAID takers (35.8 percent) versus 23 of 276 controls (8.3 percent), irrespective of H. pylori status. The two exposures were independent and synergistic: risk in H. pylori-positive NSAID takers versus H. pylori-negative non-takers was 61.1 (95 percent CI 9.98-373); H. pylori multiplied the NSAID risk 3.53-fold and NSAIDs multiplied the H. pylori risk 3.55-fold; ulcer bleeding risk rose 1.79-fold with H. pylori and 4.85-fold with NSAIDs but 6.13-fold when both were present. Used as the primary quantitative anchor that long-term NSAID therapy causes peptic ulceration.

medicalEvidence.title: Proton pump inhibitors for the prevention of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug-induced ulcers and dyspepsia.
medicalEvidence.authors: Garegnani L, Oltra G, Burgos MA, Ivaldi D, Varela LB, Díaz Menai S, Puga-Tejada M, Escobar Liquitay CM, Franco JV
medicalEvidence.summary: Cochrane systematic review of 12 randomised trials with 8,760 participants on chronic NSAID therapy. Compared with placebo, proton pump inhibitors probably reduce incident ulcers (risk ratio 0.29, 95 percent CI 0.23-0.36; 11 studies, 7,022 participants; moderate-certainty evidence) and may reduce ulcer complications (risk ratio 0.33, 95 percent CI 0.10-1.07; low certainty), while probably producing only a slight reduction in dyspepsia measured continuously and having little or no demonstrable effect on dyspepsia as a dichotomous outcome (very low certainty). Cited as intervention-response evidence that acid-dependent NSAID gastroduodenal injury is causal and preventable. LIMITATION, disclosed: certainty of evidence was low or very low for most outcomes and several included studies were at high risk of bias.

cfrCitations: 38 CFR § 4.114 (DC 7304 peptic ulcer disease; DC 7307 chronic gastritis rated as DC 7304)

secondaryCondition: Osteonecrosis (avascular necrosis) of the femoral head, glucocorticoid-associated
secondaryDiagnosticCode: No dedicated 38 CFR Part 4 diagnostic code exists for osteonecrosis of the femoral head. Evaluate the residuals under § 4.71a — hip limitation of motion and ankylosis codes DC 5250 through 5254, with painful motion under § 4.59 and, where the process has produced secondary degenerative arthrosis, on limitation of motion as § 4.71a DC 5003 directs; after total hip arthroplasty, DC 5054 (hip, resurfacing or replacement) governs. Where a code is required for the active bone disease itself, evaluate by analogy under §§ 4.20 and 4.27, with the analogous code selected and confirmed by the rating activity
primaryCondition: Rheumatoid arthritis (service-connected inflammatory polyarthritis) requiring chronic systemic glucocorticoid therapy
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.71a, DC 5002 (multi-joint arthritis, except post-traumatic and gout, 2 or more joints, as an active process — Note (1) to DC 5002 names rheumatoid arthritis among the conditions rated under it) for the active process, with chronic residuals rated under DC 5003; the steroid therapy is the treatment of that service-connected disability
etiologicalMechanism: WHY THE FEMORAL HEAD. The adult femoral head is supplied principally by the lateral and medial epiphyseal arteries derived from the medial circumflex femoral artery as it passes the posterior femoral neck, with only limited and variable contribution from the artery of the ligamentum teres. The subchondral bone is therefore a vascular watershed with almost no collateral reserve, and it is enclosed in a rigid spherical shell whose only route of venous egress is the same narrow posterior corridor. Any process that raises intraosseous pressure, obstructs the sinusoidal circulation, or impairs the arterial supply is concentrated precisely at the segment that must bear the greatest load per unit area. That anatomy is why the femoral head, and not other bones, is the classic glucocorticoid osteonecrosis target. THE GLUCOCORTICOID PATHO CASCADE. Glucocorticoids act on bone and marrow through several convergent mechanisms. (1) Direct cellular toxicity to the osteocyte and osteoblast lineage: glucocorticoids suppress Wnt/beta-catenin signalling and induce apoptosis of osteocytes and osteoblasts, which both removes the mechanical-sensing network that normally repairs subchondral microdamage and abolishes new bone formation at the site. (2) Marrow adipogenesis and mechanical obstruction: glucocorticoids shift marrow stromal cell differentiation from the osteoblastic toward the adipocytic lineage, so the marrow fat volume expands within a rigid compartment; enlarged adipocytes compress the thin-walled sinusoidal veins, raising intraosseous pressure in a compartment with no compliance. (3) Fat embolism and lipid micro-occlusion of the subchondral arterioles and capillaries, a well-described histological finding in steroid-associated osteonecrosis. (4) Impaired angiogenesis and repair capacity, with reduced expression of angiogenic signalling and failure to revascularise the ischaemic segment. (5) A hypercoagulable, hypofibrinolytic state with impaired sinusoidal flow. The end result is a self-reinforcing loop: ischaemia causes osteocyte death, dead bone loses its repair capacity and trabecular architecture, repetitive loading produces subchondral microfracture, the subchondral plate collapses, the articular surface loses its spherical congruity, and secondary degenerative arthrosis of the hip follows — usually with a characteristic precollapse window measured in months to a couple of years in which the process is visible on MRI but the radiograph is still normal. THE DOSE PATTERN, WHICH IS THE DECISIVE POINT FOR THE MEDICATION-SIDE-EFFECT ARM. The risk is carried predominantly by short-term high-dose exposure rather than by cumulative dose. The ARCO consensus criteria for glucocorticoid-associated osteonecrosis require a history of more than 2 grams of prednisolone or its equivalent within a three-month period, diagnosis within two years of that use, and the absence of other risk factors — a formal case definition that both identifies the exposure and builds in the exclusion requirement. Meta-analysis in systemic lupus erythematosus, the best-quantified autoimmune cohort, found that pulse steroid therapy (odds ratio 2.02), an initial dose greater than 60 mg/day (odds ratio 4.19) and a maximum daily dose greater than 50 mg (standardised mean difference 0.42) each significantly increased the risk, whereas cumulative glucocorticoid dose showed no significant association (P = 0.14). That asymmetry is diagnostically useful: it permits a nexus opinion to rest on a documented pulse of high-dose steroid therapy given for the service-connected arthritis even where total lifetime exposure looks modest, and it equally warns that a veteran on a stable long-term low-dose regimen cannot have causation inferred from cumulative quantity alone. SECTION 3.310(a) ANALYSIS. This is a medication side effect pleaded under § 3.310(a), not aggravation under § 3.310(b). The glucocorticoid was prescribed to treat the service-connected rheumatoid arthritis, so it is part of that disability's management and its foreseeable consequences are within the reach of proximate cause. The statute contains no requirement of medical fault and no requirement that the therapy have been unnecessary, so the fact that the steroid course was appropriate, guideline-concordant and clinically indicated does not defeat the claim; it only means the analysis is the causation analysis. Note also the distinction from an increase in severity: the osteonecrosis is a new and separate disability, not a worsening of the arthritis, so the baseline-severity machinery of § 3.310(b) does not govern. MEETING THE AT LEAST AS LIKELY AS NOT STANDARD. The opinion must establish: (1) a service-connected inflammatory arthritis rated under DC 5002 with chronic residuals under DC 5003; (2) a documented glucocorticoid exposure history identifying the drug, dose, route and dates, ideally showing a pulse or initial high-dose regimen within the ARCO window rather than an unquantified statement that steroids were used; (3) osteonecrosis documented by MRI in the pre-collapse stage or by radiography once advanced, at a site and stage that explains the veteran's pain and limp; (4) an interval between the steroid exposure and the diagnosis consistent with the ARCO two-year expectation, or an explicit explanation of the longer interval; and (5) a rigorous exclusion of the competing causes, because the ARCO criteria require the absence of other risk factors and a veteran with a material competing exposure does not fit the formal case definition. Those competing causes are alcohol abuse, heavy smoking, hypertriglyceridaemia and hypercholesterolaemia, prior hip trauma or surgery, developmental hip dysplasia, sickle cell disease and other haemoglobinopathies, Gaucher disease, decompression sickness, human immunodeficiency virus and antiretroviral therapy, organ transplantation, and radiotherapy. The inflammatory disease itself is also a contributor and must be acknowledged: in the lupus meta-analysis, vasculitis (odds ratio 3.17), thrombocytopenia (1.69), arthritis (1.88), Raynaud phenomenon (1.60) and hypertension (1.48) were independent risk factors for osteonecrosis, indicating that immune-complex vasculopathy contributes to the same microvascular end point. Those figures are derived from a lupus cohort and are offered as an analogy to inflammatory arthritis generally, not as a rheumatoid arthritis estimate. LIMITATIONS DISCLOSED ON THE FACE OF THE OPINION. First, the ARCO criteria are classification criteria developed by expert consensus to standardise research studies; they are not a diagnostic test and passing or failing them does not by itself decide an individual claim. Second, the dose-pattern findings come predominantly from systemic lupus erythematosus populations, and the exact risk thresholds cannot be transported to rheumatoid arthritis without qualification. Third, causality in the individual case still requires exclusion of alcohol and metabolic co-factors that are common in the veteran population, and where those are present the case is properly pleaded as glucocorticoid-associated osteonecrosis with contributing factors rather than as a pure single-cause attribution. Fourth, the disease is often silent until collapse, so the absence of earlier complaints does not weigh against the nexus and should not be used to argue that the condition was pre-existing. Fifth, no Part 4 code names the disease, so the rating pathway is a matter of analogy and residuals and must be fixed by the rating activity rather than by this mapping. Sixth, this mapping is a knowledge-base hypothesis only; it does not adjudicate an individual claim and the diagnostic codes must be confirmed by a qualified rating specialist against the current schedule before reliance.

medicalEvidence.title: Etiologic Classification Criteria of ARCO on Femoral Head Osteonecrosis Part 1: Glucocorticoid-Associated Osteonecrosis.
medicalEvidence.authors: Yoon BH, Jones LC, Chen CH, Cheng EY, Cui Q, Drescher W, Fukushima W, Gangji V, Goodman SB, Ha YC, Hernigou P, Hungerford M, Iorio R, Jo WL, Khanduja V, Kim H, Kim SY, Kim TY, Lee HY, Lee MS, Lee YK, Lee YJ, Mont MA, Sakai T, Sugano N, Takao M, Yamamoto T, Koo KH
medicalEvidence.summary: International Delphi consensus of 28 osteonecrosis experts from 8 countries establishing the formal case definition for glucocorticoid-associated osteonecrosis of the femoral head: (1) a history of glucocorticoid use exceeding 2 grams of prednisolone or its equivalent within a three-month period; (2) osteonecrosis diagnosed within two years of that use; and (3) the absence of other risk factors besides glucocorticoids. Used to define the exposure threshold and the temporal window that a nexus opinion should test against, and cited for the express requirement that competing risk factors be excluded. LIMITATION, disclosed: these are research classification criteria reached by expert consensus, not a diagnostic test and not an evidentiary standard.

medicalEvidence.title: Prevalence of Nontraumatic Osteonecrosis of the Femoral Head and its Associated Risk Factors in the Chinese Population: Results from a Nationally Representative Survey.
medicalEvidence.authors: Zhao DW, Yu M, Hu K, Wang W, Yang L, Wang BJ, Gao XH, Guo YM, Xu YQ, Wei YS, Tian SM, Yang F, Wang N, Huang SB, Xie H, Wei XW, Jiang HS, Zang YQ, Ai J, Chen YL, Lei GH, Li YJ, Tian G, Li ZS, Cao Y, Ma L
medicalEvidence.summary: Nationally representative survey of 30,030 respondents with bilateral hip radiography and/or MRI. Nontraumatic osteonecrosis of the femoral head was diagnosed in 218 subjects (0.725 percent), an estimated 8.12 million people aged 15 years and over, with higher prevalence in males (1.02 versus 0.51 percent, P < 0.001). Multivariate regression identified glucocorticoid intake, alcohol abuse, heavy smoking, high triglycerides, total cholesterol, LDL and non-HDL cholesterol, male sex, urban residence, family history of osteonecrosis, overweight and obesity as significantly associated with increased risk; the authors note that the condition shares risk factors with atherosclerosis. Used to establish population frequency and, critically, the competing risk factors that any individual nexus opinion must exclude. LIMITATION, disclosed: cross-sectional association data from one national population, not an individual causal model.

medicalEvidence.title: Population characteristics, glucocorticoid dosage, and risk factors for osteonecrosis of the femoral head in systemic lupus erythematosus: a Systematic Review and meta-analysis.
medicalEvidence.authors: Zhang J, Zhang J, Dong Y, Li N, Li J, Wen Y, Yan J, Tan B, Yan Y
medicalEvidence.summary: Thirty-five cohort and case-control studies with 11,356 participants. On glucocorticoid therapy, pulse steroid therapy (odds ratio 2.02, P < 0.00001), an initial dose above 60 mg/day (odds ratio 4.19, P < 0.0001), a maximum daily dose above 50 mg (standardised mean difference 0.42, P = 0.0002) and higher average daily intake (SMD 0.32, P = 0.004) significantly increased risk, whereas cumulative glucocorticoid dose showed no significant association (P = 0.14); the authors conclude that short-term high-dose exposure, not cumulative dose, is the core medication-related risk. Independent non-steroid risk factors in the same cohort were vasculitis (odds ratio 3.17), hypertension (1.48), Raynaud phenomenon (1.60), thrombocytopenia (1.69), arthritis (1.88) and positive antiphospholipid antibodies (2.00). Used for the dose-pattern finding that is decisive for the medication-side-effect arm, and for the list of disease-related contributing factors. LIMITATION, disclosed: the population is lupus, not rheumatoid arthritis, so the dose thresholds and the non-steroid risk factors are offered by analogy only.

secondaryCondition: Seizure disorder (unprovoked post-traumatic seizures, i.e. post-traumatic epilepsy)
secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.124a, DC 8910 (epilepsy, grand mal), DC 8911 (epilepsy, petit mal), DC 8912 (epilepsy, Jacksonian and focal motor or sensory) or DC 8914 (epilepsy, psychomotor), rated under the General Rating Formula for Major and Minor Epileptic Seizures; minimum evaluation is 10 percent where continuous medication is shown necessary for control, and that rating is not to be combined with any other rating for epilepsy
primaryCondition: Residuals of traumatic brain injury (service-connected traumatic brain injury)
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.124a, DC 8045 (residuals of traumatic brain injury), evaluated under the table titled Evaluation of Cognitive Impairment and Other Residuals of TBI Not Otherwise Classified
etiologicalMechanism: THE REGULATORY PRESUMPTION, WHICH IS THE STRONGEST FEATURE OF THIS PATHWAY. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(d)(1), in a veteran who has a service-connected traumatic brain injury the listed conditions shall be held to be the proximate result of that injury in the absence of clear evidence to the contrary; subparagraph (d)(1)(ii) names unprovoked seizures following moderate or severe traumatic brain injury. Two consequences follow and both must be understood before the medical evidence is discussed. First, unlike the dementia entries in (d)(1)(iii) which are confined to a 15-year manifestation window, and unlike depression in (d)(1)(iv) which is confined to 3 years after moderate or severe injury or 12 months after mild injury, the unprovoked-seizure provision carries no stated time limit at all. A veteran with a service-connected moderate or severe traumatic brain injury who develops unprovoked seizures years later therefore does not need a case-by-case medical nexus opinion to establish service connection; the regulation concedes the proximate-result element and the opinion's real work is to establish the severity of the original injury and to exclude the clear evidence to the contrary. Second, § 3.310(d)(2) provides that neither the severity levels nor the time limits preclude a finding of service connection for conditions shown by evidence to be proximately due to the service-connected brain injury, and that where a claim does not meet the requirements of (d)(1) the claim is developed and decided under generally applicable principles without regard to (d)(1). A mild traumatic brain injury is therefore not a dead end; it moves the claim onto the ordinary § 3.310(a) causation track, where the epidemiological evidence below carries the burden. DETERMINING SEVERITY, WHICH IS THE PRACTICAL ADJUDICATIVE STEP. Section 3.310(d)(3) supplies the table: mild requires loss of consciousness of 0 to 30 minutes, alteration of consciousness from a moment up to 24 hours, post-traumatic amnesia of 0 to 1 day, and a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 13 to 15; moderate requires loss of consciousness greater than 30 minutes and less than 24 hours, post-traumatic amnesia greater than 1 and less than 7 days, and a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 9 to 12; severe requires loss of consciousness greater than 24 hours, post-traumatic amnesia greater than 7 days, and a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 3 to 8. Structural imaging may be normal or abnormal at the moderate and severe levels. The regulation then states that severity is determined by the findings at the time of injury or shortly thereafter rather than by the current level of functioning, that a veteran is not required to meet every criterion under a severity level to be classified at that level, and that where criteria in more than one category are met the injury is ranked at the highest level in which a criterion is met. All of that means the contemporaneous emergency department, theatre or field record is the decisive document, and later records showing good recovery years afterwards must not be used to demote the injury to mild. THE MECHANISM. Post-traumatic epileptogenesis begins with the primary mechanical event and continues for years. Cortical contusion and subdural haematoma cause direct neuronal loss and axonal shearing; the breakdown of the blood-brain barrier exposes neurons to serum albumin and other proteins that alter astrocytic potassium and glutamate handling; extravasated blood leaves haemosiderin and free iron in the cortex, which is a potent driver of reactive oxygen species and of persistent local inflammation; and reactive gliosis forms a scar that isolates but does not silence the injured cortex. The functional consequence is a failure of the excitatory-inhibitory balance: selective loss of GABAergic inhibitory interneurons in the perilesional cortex, upregulation of excitatory glutamatergic signalling and of voltage-gated sodium and calcium channels, and sprouting of aberrant recurrent excitatory collaterals produce a population of neurons that fires synchronously and uncontrollably. The latency between injury and the first unprovoked seizure — commonly months, and sometimes years — reflects the time required for these structural and network changes to mature, which is why a long interval is expected rather than anomalous and why an opinion should not treat a several-year gap as evidence against causation. THE EPIDEMIOLOGY, WITH ITS OWN WEAKNESSES STATED. The population-based Olmsted County study of 4,541 patients found an overall standardised incidence ratio for unprovoked seizures after traumatic brain injury of 3.1 (95 percent CI 2.5-3.8), rising to 17.0 (95 percent CI 12.3-23.6) after severe injury, with moderate injury at 2.9 (95 percent CI 1.9-4.1) and mild injury at 1.5 (95 percent CI 1.0-2.2) with no excess beyond five years; the risk factors identified on multivariable analysis were brain contusion with subdural haematoma, skull fracture, loss of consciousness or amnesia lasting more than a day, and age of 65 years or older. A national cohort of 1,605,216 people confirmed the severity relationship (relative risk 2.22, 95 percent CI 2.07-2.38 after mild injury and 7.40, 95 percent CI 6.16-8.89 after severe injury), showed that the excess risk persisted beyond 10 years (relative risk 1.51 after mild and 4.29 after severe injury), and found a higher risk in those injured above the age of 15. A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 studies and 242,803 patients found a pooled incidence of post-traumatic seizures of 7.2 percent (95 percent CI 5.4-9.3) but substantial heterogeneity (I squared 98 percent) and a pooled relative risk for severe traumatic brain injury of 2.98 that was not statistically significant (95 percent CI 0.81-11.01, P = 0.08), with the authors identifying inadequate seizure ascertainment in the included studies as a major limitation. The epidemiological support is therefore strong for the direction and the severity gradient, and weaker for any precise individual probability; a nexus opinion should rely on the gradient and the mechanism, not on a claimed percentage that the literature will not support. SECTION 3.310(a) AND THE AT LEAST AS LIKELY AS NOT STANDARD. Where § 3.310(d)(1)(ii) does not apply because the injury was mild, or where the presumption is rebutted by clear evidence to the contrary, the opinion must establish: (1) a service-connected traumatic brain injury rated under DC 8045 with the contemporaneous severity indicators documented; (2) a clinical diagnosis of epilepsy by a neurologist, supported where possible by electroencephalography, and correctly characterised — focal aware, focal impaired awareness, focal to bilateral tonic-clonic, or generalised — because DC 8912 (Jacksonian and focal motor or sensory) and DC 8910 (grand mal) describe different seizure types and the General Rating Formula distinguishes major from minor seizures, with the predominating type controlling; (3) a chronological and anatomical concordance between the site of injury, the electroencephalographic focus and the seizure semiology, which is the single most probative individual finding available; (4) exclusion of competing causes, namely pre-existing epilepsy, alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, metabolic derangement, central nervous system infection, brain tumour, stroke, medication or drug effect, sleep deprivation-induced seizures in a patient with a pre-existing epilepsy syndrome, and psychogenic non-epileptic spells, because the presumption applies only to unprovoked seizures and the regulation itself preserves a clear-evidence-to-the-contrary escape; and (5) where the veteran had a seizure disorder before the traumatic brain injury, a recognition that the correct posture is aggravation under § 3.310(b) with a baseline severity established by medical evidence predating the worsening, not causation. SEPARATE RATING AND PYRIMIDING. The rating schedule resolves the duplication question in the claimant's favour by its own text. Diagnostic code 8045 directs that physical dysfunction including seizures be evaluated under an appropriate diagnostic code, and the closing paragraph of DC 8045 requires that each condition be evaluated separately so long as the same signs and symptoms are not used to support more than one evaluation, with combination under § 4.25. A post-traumatic epilepsy rating under DC 8910 through 8914 is therefore contemplated by the schedule rather than barred by § 4.14, provided the seizure manifestations are not simultaneously used as the subjective-symptoms facet of the DC 8045 table. Note (1) to the 8045 table reinforces this by forbidding more than one evaluation based on the same manifestations. LIMITATIONS DISCLOSED ON THE FACE OF THE OPINION. First, the 2026 meta-analysis found substantial unexplained heterogeneity and a pooled severe-injury relative risk that did not reach statistical significance, so the quantitative support is weaker than a single favourable figure would suggest and no numeric probability should be asserted in an opinion. Second, the population-based studies measure unprovoked seizures after injury in general populations; they do not model a veteran's individual exposures, and the Olmsted County cohort spans an era of materially different acute neurotrauma care. Third, the presumption in § 3.310(d)(1)(ii) applies to unprovoked seizures only, so any opinion that elides the provoked-versus-unprovoked distinction is unreliable, and the regulation expressly permits rebuttal by clear evidence to the contrary. Fourth, this mapping is a knowledge-base hypothesis only; it does not adjudicate an individual claim and the diagnostic codes must be confirmed by a qualified rating specialist against the current schedule before reliance. Fifth, and separately, the knowledge-base catalog contains both a published epilepsy identity and a draft seizure-disorder identity with no authored mappings; this row is written against the draft identity, and a maintainer decision is required so that the two do not become duplicate concepts in the graph.

medicalEvidence.title: A population-based study of seizures after traumatic brain injuries.
medicalEvidence.authors: Annegers JF, Hauser WA, Coan SP, Rocca WA
medicalEvidence.summary: Population-based cohort of 4,541 patients with traumatic brain injury in Olmsted County, Minnesota, followed for the occurrence of unprovoked seizures. The overall standardised incidence ratio was 3.1 (95 percent CI 2.5-3.8), rising with injury severity to 2.9 (95 percent CI 1.9-4.1) after moderate injury and 17.0 (95 percent CI 12.3-23.6) after severe injury, with no excess beyond five years after mild injury. Multivariable risk factors were brain contusion with subdural haematoma, skull fracture, loss of consciousness or amnesia exceeding one day, and age 65 years or older. This is the primary anchor for the severity gradient on which the § 3.310(d) structure depends. LIMITATION, disclosed: historical cohort from a single county, with treatment eras that predate modern neurocritical care.

medicalEvidence.title: Long-term risk of epilepsy after traumatic brain injury in children and young adults: a population-based cohort study.
medicalEvidence.authors: Christensen J, Pedersen MG, Pedersen CB, Sidenius P, Olsen J, Vestergaard M
medicalEvidence.summary: Nationwide Danish cohort of 1,605,216 people followed for epilepsy after traumatic brain injury. Relative risk was 2.22 (95 percent CI 2.07-2.38) after mild injury and 7.40 (95 percent CI 6.16-8.89) after severe injury, with skull fracture conferring a relative risk of 2.17 (95 percent CI 1.73-2.71); the excess risk persisted more than 10 years after injury (relative risk 1.51 after mild and 4.29 after severe injury) and was higher in those injured above 15 years of age. Cited for the long-term persistence of risk, which is what makes the absence of a time limit in § 3.310(d)(1)(ii) medically coherent rather than anomalous. LIMITATION, disclosed: observational cohort with register-based seizure ascertainment and residual confounding.

medicalEvidence.title: Clinical risk factors for post-traumatic seizures: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
medicalEvidence.authors: Viaroli E, Gillespie C, Mee H, Chedid Y, Corper S, Joannides A, Menon D, Mohan M, Needham E, Newcombe V, Servadei F, Timofeev I, Kolias A, Hutchinson PJA
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 studies with 242,803 patients. Pooled incidence of post-traumatic seizures was 7.2 percent (95 percent CI 5.4-9.3) with very high heterogeneity (I squared 98 percent), and the pooled relative risk for severe traumatic brain injury was 2.98 (95 percent CI 0.81-11.01, P = 0.08), which did not reach statistical significance; individual studies identified severe injury and lower Glasgow Coma Scale, subdural haematoma, cortical contusions and age as multivariable risk factors. The authors identify inadequate ascertainment of seizures across studies as a major limitation. Cited as the most recent synthesis and, importantly, cited against overstatement: it supports the severity gradient and the clinical risk-factor list while showing that the pooled quantitative estimate is unstable. LIMITATION, disclosed: the pooled severe-injury effect did not reach significance and no numeric probability should be asserted from it.
